At the steps where we had brought him aboard, and ever since then, I had watched carefully for any sign that someone suspected us. I had seen nothing. We had certainly not been followed, and no boat was following us or keeping alongside us now. If one had been, I would have pulled in to shore, forcing it either to go past or to show what it wanted. But we kept moving without any sign of interference.

He wore his boat-cloak and, as I have said, looked perfectly at home in the scene. Strangely, he was the least worried of us all, though perhaps his miserable past explained that. He did care about what happened: he told me he hoped to live long enough to see his gentleman become one of the finest gentlemen in a foreign country. Nor, as I understood him, was he simply willing to accept whatever happened. He just did not believe in worrying about danger before it arrived. When it came, he faced it, but until then he would not trouble himself.

“If you knew, dear boy,” he told me, “what it means to sit here beside my dear boy and have a smoke, after spending day after day shut inside four walls, you’d envy me. But you don’t know what it means.”

“I think I understand the pleasure of being free,” I answered.

“Ah,” he said, shaking his head seriously. “But you don’t understand it the way I do. You’d have to have been locked up, dear boy, to know it as I do—but I’m not going to get gloomy.”

It seemed strange to me that he had risked his freedom, and even his life, for any idea, however powerful. Then I wondered whether a life of freedom without danger was so unlike everything he knew that it could never mean to him what it meant to someone else. I was not far wrong, for after smoking a little he said:

“You see, dear boy, when I was over there, on the other side of the world, I was always looking towards this side. Being there felt empty, even though I was getting rich. Everyone knew Magwitch. Magwitch could come and Magwitch could go, and nobody gave him a thought. They aren’t so easy about me here, dear boy—or they wouldn’t be if they knew where I was.”

“If everything goes well,” I said, “in a few hours you’ll be completely free and safe again.”

“Well,” he replied, taking a long breath, “I hope so.”

“And do you think so?”

“Now, in English, e is the letter of most frequent occurrence. The succession thereafter is: a o i d h n r s t u y c f g l m w b k p q x z. So marked is the predominance of e that one seldom encounters a sentence of any considerable length in which it is not the prevailing letter.

“Thus, at the very outset, we lay a foundation for something beyond mere conjecture. The general application of this table is plain enough; for our particular cipher, however, we shall have only partial occasion for its assistance. Our most abundant character being 8, let us begin by supposing it to represent the e of the ordinary alphabet. To put this supposition to the test, we may ask whether 8 frequently occurs in pairs, since English very often doubles e—in ‘meet,’ for instance, ‘fleet,’ ‘speed,’ ‘seen,’ ‘been,’ ‘agree,’ and the like. Brief as this cryptograph is, the character appears doubled no fewer than five times.

“Let 8, then, stand for e. Of all the words in our language, ‘the’ is the commonest. We should therefore examine the writing for repeated groups of three characters, arranged in the same order and ending with 8. Repetitions of that description will in all probability signify ‘the.’ On examination we discover no fewer than seven such groups, composed of the characters ;48. We may accordingly assign t to ;, h to 4, and e to 8; the last assignment is now strongly confirmed. A considerable advance has thus been made.

“Yet the determination of a single word enables us to settle another point of great importance: the beginnings and endings of several other words. Consider, for example, the next-to-last occurrence of ;48, situated near the conclusion of the cipher. We know that the ; which follows immediately must begin a word; and of the six characters after this ‘the,’ five are already familiar to us. Let us write them in the letters which we know they signify, leaving a blank for the unknown character:

t eeth.

“We can at once reject the final ‘th’ as belonging to the word which begins with the first t. For, on trying every letter of the alphabet in the vacant place, we find that no word can be produced which includes this ‘th.’ Our inquiry is therefore reduced to

t ee,

and, passing through the alphabet again if necessary, we obtain ‘tree’ as the only possible interpretation.

But now she wished it had not happened. She thought he had drunk too much of Mr. Weston’s good wine and was sure he would begin talking nonsense.

Hoping that her own behaviour would keep him under control, she was about to speak very calmly and seriously about the weather and the night. She had barely begun, and they had scarcely passed the gate and caught up with the other carriage, when he interrupted her, took her hand, and demanded her attention. Mr. Elton was actually making an intense declaration of love to her. Seizing this precious chance, he spoke of feelings that, he claimed, she must already understand. He hoped, feared, adored her, and was ready to die if she refused him. Yet he assured himself that his deep attachment, his unequalled love, and his extraordinary passion must have some effect. In short, he was determined that she should accept him seriously and as soon as possible. There could be no doubt about it. Without hesitation, apology, or much apparent nervousness, Mr. Elton—the man she believed loved Harriet—was declaring that he loved her instead. She tried to interrupt him, but he would not stop until he had said everything. Angry though she was, she decided to control herself when she replied. She felt sure that drink must explain half this foolishness, and could therefore hope that it would last no longer than the present hour. She answered with a mixture of seriousness and playfulness that she hoped would suit his half-drunken state.

“I am very astonished, Mr. Elton. Saying this to me! You have forgotten yourself. You are confusing me with my friend. I shall gladly deliver any message you have for Miss Smith, but please say no more of this to me.”

“Miss Smith! A message to Miss Smith! What could she possibly mean?” He repeated her words so confidently, with such an exaggerated show of surprise, that she could not help answering sharply.

“Mr. Elton, this is extraordinary behaviour! There is only one explanation I can see. You are not yourself, or you could never speak this way to me, or about Harriet. Control yourself enough to say nothing more, and I will try to forget it.”

But Mr. Elton had drunk only enough wine to raise his spirits, not enough to confuse his thoughts. He knew exactly what he meant. He strongly denied her suggestion, protesting that it was deeply unfair to him. He briefly mentioned his respect for Miss Smith as her friend, while admitting his surprise that Miss Smith had been brought into the conversation at all. Then he returned to his own love and pressed her urgently for a favourable answer.
